analysis.one_liner: Bans all soybean and soybean meal imports from Argentina and Brazil.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first committee referral and died when the 108th Congress ended, with one sponsor and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to bring soybeans or soybean meal from Argentina or Brazil into the United States, including goods already sitting in warehouses. The purpose is to shield American soybean growers from foreign competition by cutting off the supply of cheaper beans from South America. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its Trade Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: American soybean farmers, who would face less competition from South American beans and could expect stronger prices for their crops. Soybean processors that crush domestic beans would also benefit from a captive supply.

how_it_helps.text: The bill outright prohibits importing soybeans (Harmonized Tariff Schedule heading 1201.00.00) or soybean meal (subheading 1208.10.00) that are products of Argentina or Brazil.
Removing competing foreign supply would support higher prices for domestically grown soybeans, benefiting U.S. growers.
The ban would also cover beans already in U.S. warehouses, by counting withdrawal from warehouse for consumption as an import.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of soybeans and soybean meal — livestock and poultry producers who use meal as animal feed, food processors, and ultimately consumers — would face higher feed and food costs from a restricted supply. Livestock and poultry are the dominant use of soybean meal in the United States, so a supply ban would raise costs across the meat and egg supply chain. It would also shut out Argentine and Brazilian growers from the U.S. market.

drawbacks.text: Blocking imports of soybeans and soybean meal would raise feed costs for livestock and poultry producers, and those costs would feed through to prices for meat, eggs, and other foods.
The bill would insulate U.S. soybean farmers from foreign competition, which means higher prices for domestic buyers rather than lower ones.
Retaliatory trade barriers are a common response to import bans, so U.S. agricultural exporters could face new restrictions abroad in response.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated on one group — American soybean growers, who would get higher prices — while the costs spread broadly across everyone who eats meat, eggs, or products made with soybean oil and meal. It is a classic protectionist trade-off: a visible benefit for a politically organized industry and a diffuse cost paid by consumers and downstream producers. On balance, the public cost outweighs the narrow benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and then its Trade Subcommittee, nothing further happened, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Latham introduced the bill in the House on February 4, 2004.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on February 4, 2004, and to the Subcommittee on Trade on February 6, 2004.
No further action was taken before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the ban never became law, livestock and poultry producers kept access to imported soybean meal, importers kept their market, and consumers avoided the higher feed-driven food prices the ban would have caused. U.S. soybean growers are worse off than they would have been under the ban.

for.name: Rep. Tom Latham
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the import ban and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over trade bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 4, 2004 and sent it to the Trade Subcommittee, then took no further action before the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote to show a partisan split; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of any party before it died in committee.

industries.note: The ban would cut off competing South American supply, pushing up prices for domestically grown soybeans. The benefit accrues to growers while the cost lands on feed and food buyers.
Soybean meal is a core animal feed, and the bill would cut off imports from two major meal-producing countries, raising feed costs for meat and egg producers and, ultimately, prices for consumers.

industries.industry: Argentine and Brazilian soybean growers and exporters
industries.note: The bill would bar their products from the U.S. market entirely. Their loss would come through higher world prices and reduced competition, not consumer harm.

Importers of South American soybeans and meal would lose their supply; domestic crushers would gain a protected market. Warehouse-stored beans would have been caught too, since withdrawing them for consumption counts as an import under the bill.
